cards.explanation: The answer is 180. King Xerxes, who reigned over 127 provinces, spends a full 180 days displaying the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness (Esther 1:4). That's about six months of show and tell, friends. I can't hold a fresh batch of cookies for six minutes before I'm showing somebody.

The answer is everyone in the citadel of Susa. The king holds a seven-day feast for all the people in the citadel of Susa, “…from the least to the greatest.” (Esther 1:5) No fancy title needed for this one, friends. If you were inside Susa's citadel, you were on the list.

The answer is False. The goblets are gold, and each one has a different design (Esther 1:7). Not one matching set in the whole garden court, friends. That's a lot of different goblets to keep track of.

The answer is whatever he desires. By order of the king, no limit was placed on the drinking, and every official of his household was to serve each man whatever he desired (Esther 1:8). The royal wine flowed freely, friends. Nobody at that feast had to count goblets.

The answer is women. Queen Vashti gives a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Xerxes (Esther 1:9). The king has his feast, and the queen has a banquet of her own, friends. Her guest list is the women.

The answer is True. The king orders the eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing her royal crown (Esther 1:11). That's a summons with a dress code attached, friends. I've gotten invitations that said "casual," and I still showed up overdressed and sweating. This one says crown, and it doesn't leave any room for guessing.

The answer is beauty. Xerxes wants her brought in to display her beauty to the people and officials. The text adds, “For she was beautiful to behold.” (Esther 1:11) That's what the king has in mind for this moment, friends.

The answer is that she refuses to come. Queen Vashti refuses to come at the king's command brought by his eunuchs (Esther 1:12). The text doesn't give her reason, so I won't make one up, friends. The command came by the eunuchs, and her answer was no.

The answer is seven. His closest advisors are seven princes of Persia and Media who had personal access to the king and ranked highest in the kingdom (Esther 1:14). That's one more group of seven in this story, friends. This passage loves that number.

The answer is law. The king asks, “According to law, what should be done with Queen Vashti…” (Esther 1:15). He asks the experts in law and justice, as the text says it was his custom to do (Esther 1:13). He goes to the legal people first, friends.

The answer is the princes and peoples of every province. Memucan says, “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but all the princes and the peoples in all the provinces of King Xerxes.” (Esther 1:16) He says it in front of the king and his princes, friends. He wants everyone in the kingdom counted in on this.

The answer is despise. Memucan says the queen's conduct will become known to all women, “…causing them to despise their husbands…” (Esther 1:17). That's what he claims will happen, friends. I'll note it's his prediction, not something the text shows us happening.

The answer is that she may never again enter the king's presence. Memucan says the decree should state “…that Vashti shall never again enter the presence of King Xerxes…” (Esther 1:19). This one is a heavy moment, friends. I think it hurts to read.

The answer is True. Memucan wants it recorded in the laws of Persia and Media “…so that it cannot be repealed…” (Esther 1:19). Once it's written there, it stays, friends. That's the opposite of a sticky note you can peel off.

The answer is that they will honor their husbands. Memucan says the edict will be heard throughout the vast kingdom, “…and so all women, from the least to the greatest, will honor their husbands.” (Esther 1:20) That's what he says will follow from the edict, friends. The text doesn't tell us how it turns out.

The answer is True. The king and his princes were pleased with this counsel, so the king did as Memucan advised (Esther 1:21). The king acted on the advice he was given, friends. Memucan's counsel became the king's move.

The answer is False. The king sent letters to all the provinces, “…to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language…” (Esther 1:22). So the letters went out in the languages of the different peoples, friends. That's a whole lot of writing from one royal pen.
